Indian Forest Act, 1927 — Section 67: Power to try offences summarily
67. Power to try offences summarily.—The District Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class specially empowered in this behalf by the 1[State Government] may try summarily, under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (5 of 1898), any forest-offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or fine not exceeding five hundred rupees, or both. STATE AMENDMENTS Maharashtra Amendment of section 67 of Act 16 of 1927.—In section 67 of the principal Act, for the words “two thousand rupees” the words “five thousand rupees” shall be substituted. [Vide Maharashtra Act 21 of 2015, s. 17]. STATE AMENDMENT Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh (UTs).— Section 67.-For the words “not exceeding six months, or fine not exceeding five hundred rupees”, substitute the words “not exceeding two years or with fine not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees”. [Vide the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization (Adaptation of Central Laws) Order, 2020, notification No. S.O. 1123(E) dated (18-3-2020).]

Question: How have the financial penalties for forest offences under Section 67 been adjusted in Maharashtra and Jammu & Kashmir/Ladakh, and what does this reflect about regional legal priorities?

chosen.content: In Maharashtra, the State Amendment (Maharashtra Act 21 of 2015) increased the maximum fine for forest offences under Section 67 from ₹500 to ₹5,000, indicating a regional emphasis on deterring violations through higher financial consequences. Meanwhile, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh (UTs) expanded the scope further by substituting the fine limit to ₹25,000 and extending the imprisonment term to *up to two years*, reflecting a more stringent approach to enforcement in these regions. These adjustments suggest that while Maharashtra prioritized escalating monetary penalties, Jammu & Kashmir/Ladakh adopted a dual strategy of combining longer incarceration with significantly higher fines, likely due to unique ecological or administrative considerations.

Under the **Indian Forest Act, 1927**, **Section 67** imposes penalties for unauthorized felling, damaging, or destroying protected trees, with standard fines ranging from **₹1,000 to ₹10,000** (or imprisonment up to **3 months**) for first offences, escalating to **₹5,000–₹25,000** (or imprisonment up to **6 months**) for repeat violations.

In **Maharashtra**, the **Maharashtra Forest Rules, 1995 (Rule 117)** and **Maharashtra Forest (Amendment) Act, 2021** have **increased penalties**—for instance, unauthorized tree felling now attracts fines up to **₹1 lakh** (or imprisonment up to **1 year**) in high-priority forest areas, reflecting a stricter enforcement stance to combat **illegal timber trade and urban encroachments**. Meanwhile, **Jammu & Kashmir/Ladakh** (under the **J&K Forest Rules, 1976, and Ladakh Forest Rules, 2021**) have **higher penalties in ecologically sensitive zones**, such as fines of **₹2 lakh–₹5 lakh** for offences near **protected forests or wildlife corridors**, underscoring regional priorities for **conservation and climate resilience** amid unique environmental challenges (e.g., glacial melt, wildlife corridors).

This **regional variation** highlights how **Maharashtra prioritizes suppression of urban encroachments and commercial timber crimes**, while **J&K/Ladakh emphasizes protection of fragile ecosystems**—a reflection of **local ecological threats and governance approaches**.
